subject: [PATCH for-7.5 0/5] memcg: clean up memory.high enforcement

reviews.author: Harry Yoo
reviews.summary: Reviewer Harry Yoo noted that try_charge_memcg() is doing too much and suggested breaking out the memory.high enforcement into a new function, memcg_enforce_high(), to improve readability and maintainability.
reviews.raw_body:
On Sat, Oct 10, 2026 at 02:09:53PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> try_charge_memcg() does a lot. It charges the page counters, reclaims
> when a limit is hit, may call the OOM killer, and at the end it checks
> and enforces memory.high. Move the memory.high part into a new function,
> memcg_enforce_high(), so that try_charge_memcg() is shorter and the
> memory.high code is easier to read and change.
> 
> The code and its comments move as they are. The only difference is that
> the new function gets allow_spinning from gfp_mask itself.
> 
> No functional change.
> ---

Missing Signed-off-by: ?

Otherwise LGTM.
Reviewed-by: Harry Yoo (Meta) <harry@kernel.org>

-- 
Cheers,
Harry / Hyeonggon

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
reviews.summary: The author addressed concerns about the patch's behavior and implementation details. Specifically, they clarified that the high_work worker can queue itself from its own reclaim without delaying the actual charge request, but may waste CPU if high reclaim is not successful. They also explained why they chose to keep a separate check for memory.high enforcement in the high enforcement function, rather than unifying it with the existing check in try_charge_memcg().

On Wed, Oct 14, 2026 at 01:39:06PM +0200, Michal Hocko wrote:
> On Sat 10-10-26 14:09:56, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> > Kernel threads and remote chargers use high_work when memory.high is
> > exceeded. Their allocations during reclaim can also charge memory,
> > for example when zswap stores a page.
> > 
> > Without a check, the high_work worker can queue itself from its own
> > reclaim. The pending bit is cleared before high_work runs, so each run
> > can queue another run.
> 
> What does that mean really? Does this delays the actual run?

It will not delay the actual charge request. This mainly means that we keep
enqueing the high reclaim work even from high reclaim context and can
potentially keep wasting CPU if high reclaim is not very successful.

>  
> > Skip memory.high enforcement for charges from task context with
> > PF_MEMALLOC set when they would use high_work. This covers kernel
> > threads and remote charges. The memory is still charged. Interrupt
> > charges keep their current path.
> > 
> > In a VM with incompressible zswap data, the worker queued itself 163 times
> > without this check.
> > 
> > Signed-off-by: Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev>
> 
> The patch itself looks OK. I am wondering whether we can unify the check
> with the existing one which forces the allocation through in main
> charging path.

The force charge (and ENOMEM) paths bypass the memory.high enforcement
altogether. Only successful charges (done_restock label) goes through
memory.high enforcement. So, even if we move this check in try_charge_memcg, it
will still be a separate check before calling high enforcement function. I think
this check is very high_work specific and better to be in the high enforcement
function.

very subtle and most probably unexpected. If we decide to remove it, we should
do it in a separate patch. Actually I am working on a followup series where I
plan to remove the sync enforcement of memory.high and put high enforcement on
the code paths which can potentially do a lot of allocation within a single
kernel entry.

2026-10-12.patch_summary: This patch series cleans up the enforcement of memory.high limits in Linux by moving it to a separate function and using a worker for kernel threads and remote charges. The changes aim to improve performance by avoiding unnecessary reclaiming and sleeping during charges, and also fix issues with high handler usage. The patches modify the memcg_enforce_high() function, add handling for kernel threads and remote charges, introduce a guard against queuing work from PF_MEMALLOC tasks, and simplify the scan and comments.

reviews.author: Michal Hocko
reviews.summary: Reviewer Michal Hocko noted that try_charge_memcg() is doing too many things, including charging page counters, reclaiming when a limit is hit, calling the OOM killer, and enforcing memory.high. He suggested moving the memory.high enforcement into a new function, memcg_enforce_high(), to make the code shorter and easier to read.
reviews.raw_body:
On Sat 10-10-26 14:09:53, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> try_charge_memcg() does a lot. It charges the page counters, reclaims
> when a limit is hit, may call the OOM killer, and at the end it checks
> and enforces memory.high. Move the memory.high part into a new function,
> memcg_enforce_high(), so that try_charge_memcg() is shorter and the
> memory.high code is easier to read and change.
> 
> The code and its comments move as they are. The only difference is that
> the new function gets allow_spinning from gfp_mask itself.
> 
> No functional change.

Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
Thanks!

> ---
>  mm/memcontrol.c | 125 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++----------------------
>  1 file changed, 69 insertions(+), 56 deletions(-)
> 
> diff --git a/mm/memcontrol.c b/mm/memcontrol.c
> index aad0498a7bd6..20c5dfe1a894 100644
> --- a/mm/memcontrol.c
> +++ b/mm/memcontrol.c
> @@ -2696,6 +2696,74 @@ void __mem_cgroup_handle_over_high(gfp_t gfp_mask)
>  	css_put(&memcg->css);
>  }
>  
> +/*
> + * Called after @nr_pages were charged to @memcg. If @memcg or one of its
> + * ancestors is over memory.high or memory.swap.high, start reclaim or slow
> + * down the task.
> + */
> +static void memcg_enforce_high(struct mem_cgroup *memcg, unsigned int nr_pages,
> +			       gfp_t gfp_mask)
> +{
> +	bool allow_spinning = gfpflags_allow_spinning(gfp_mask);
> +
> +	/*
> +	 * If the hierarchy is above the normal consumption range, schedule
> +	 * reclaim on returning to userland.  We can perform reclaim here
> +	 * if __GFP_RECLAIM but let's always punt for simplicity and so that
> +	 * GFP_KERNEL can consistently be used during reclaim.  @memcg is
> +	 * not recorded as it most likely matches current's and won't
> +	 * change in the meantime.  As high limit is checked again before
> +	 * reclaim, the cost of mismatch is negligible.
> +	 */
> +	do {
> +		bool mem_high, swap_high;
> +
> +		mem_high = page_counter_read(&memcg->memory) >
> +			READ_ONCE(memcg->memory.high);
> +		swap_high = page_counter_read(&memcg->swap) >
> +			READ_ONCE(memcg->swap.high);
> +
> +		/* Don't bother a random interrupted task */
> +		if (!in_task()) {
> +			if (mem_high) {
> +				if (allow_spinning)
> +					schedule_work(&memcg->high_work);
> +				else
> +					irq_work_queue(&memcg->high_irq_work);
> +				break;
> +			}
> +			continue;
> +		}
> +
> +		if (mem_high || swap_high) {
> +			/*
> +			 * The allocating tasks in this cgroup will need to do
> +			 * reclaim or be throttled to prevent further growth
> +			 * of the memory or swap footprints.
> +			 *
> +			 * Target some best-effort fairness between the tasks,
> +			 * and distribute reclaim work and delay penalties
> +			 * based on how much each task is actually allocating.
> +			 */
> +			current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high += nr_pages;
> +			set_notify_resume(current);
> +			break;
> +		}
> +	} while ((memcg = parent_mem_cgroup(memcg)));
> +
> +	/*
> +	 * Reclaim is set up above to be called from the userland
> +	 * return path. But also attempt synchronous reclaim to avoid
> +	 * excessive overrun while the task is still inside the
> +	 * kernel. If this is successful, the return path will see it
> +	 * when it rechecks the overage and simply bail out.
> +	 */
> +	if (current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high > MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH &&
> +	    !(current->flags & PF_MEMALLOC) &&
> +	    gfpflags_allow_blocking(gfp_mask))
> +		__mem_cgroup_handle_over_high(gfp_mask);
> +}
> +
>  static int try_charge_memcg(struct mem_cgroup *memcg, gfp_t gfp_mask,
>  			    unsigned int nr_pages)
>  {
> @@ -2853,62 +2921,7 @@ static int try_charge_memcg(struct mem_cgroup *memcg, gfp_t gfp_mask,
>  	if (batch > nr_pages)
>  		refill_stock(memcg, batch - nr_pages);
>  
> -	/*
> -	 * If the hierarchy is above the normal consumption range, schedule
> -	 * reclaim on returning to userland.  We can perform reclaim here
> -	 * if __GFP_RECLAIM but let's always punt for simplicity and so that
> -	 * GFP_KERNEL can consistently be used during reclaim.  @memcg is
> -	 * not recorded as it most likely matches current's and won't
> -	 * change in the meantime.  As high limit is checked again before
> -	 * reclaim, the cost of mismatch is negligible.
> -	 */
> -	do {
> -		bool mem_high, swap_high;
> -
> -		mem_high = page_counter_read(&memcg->memory) >
> -			READ_ONCE(memcg->memory.high);
> -		swap_high = page_counter_read(&memcg->swap) >
> -			READ_ONCE(memcg->swap.high);

> -			}

> -			 * Target some best-effort fairness between the tasks,
> -			 * and distribute reclaim work and delay penalties
> -			 * based on how much each task is actually allocating.

> -			current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high += batch;
> -			set_notify_resume(current);
> -			break;
> -		}

On Sat 10-10-26 14:09:54, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> Kernel threads never return to userspace, so deferred memory.high
> reclaim does not run. Reclaim and throttling during a charge can also
> delay work they do for other tasks.
> 
> Treat kernel threads like interrupts. Queue high_work for the first
> cgroup over memory.high and skip reclaim and throttling in the charging
> thread.
> 
> User workers created by create_io_thread() and vhost_task_create() keep
> their current behavior. Vhost kernel threads use the new path, even when
> they borrow the owner's mm.
> 
> The worker requests a fixed batch of pages each time. A fast allocator
> can keep usage well above memory.high. Kernel threads also skip
> memory.swap.high throttling and its high-event reporting. The memory.max
> and memory.swap.max checks stay the same.
> 
> Suggested-by: Tejun Heo <tj@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev>

yes this makes sense as a general improvemnt.

Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>

2026-10-14.patch_summary: This patch series cleans up the enforcement of memory.high limits in Linux by moving it to a separate function and using a worker for kernel threads and remote charges. The changes aim to improve performance by avoiding unnecessary reclaiming and sleeping during charges, and also fix issues with high handler usage. The patches modify the memcg_enforce_high() function, add handling for kernel threads and remote charges, introduce a guard against queuing work from PF_MEMALLOC tasks, and simplify the scan and comments.
